entry.title: The St. Petersburg Paradox, Re-Run Over Time

link.title: The St. Petersburg Paradox, Re-Run Over Time

entry.content:
I was recently trying to explain the St. Petersburg paradox to my uncle from memory during a walk in the park. The setup is a deceptively simple coin-tossing game.

A fair coin is flipped until it lands heads for the first time. If heads appears on the 1st toss, you win $2. If on the 2nd, $4. If on the 3rd, $8, and so on, with the payout doubling each time.

What is a fair price to pay to play this game?

The expected payoff is famously, and confusingly, infinite. Each outcome contributes its probability times its payout, and every one of those terms is worth exactly one dollar.

\[\mathbb{E}[X] = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\cdot \$2 + \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot \$4 + \left(\frac{1}{8}\right)\cdot \$8 + \dots = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^n} \cdot 2^n = \$1 + \$1 + \$1 + \dots = \infty\]

A purely “rational” actor, according to classical theory, should pay any finite price to play. Nobody would. Most people offer a few dollars, and as I explained this, I found myself questioning the standard explanation.

The Classical “Solution”

The classic solution, proposed by Daniel Bernoulli in 1738, is that people don’t value money linearly. An extra dollar matters less the wealthier you are. Model this diminishing marginal utility with a logarithm and the expected utility of the game becomes finite, which justifies a small price.

Expected utility rests on the von Neumann-Morgenstern axioms, and Kelly-growth arguments single out the logarithm in particular. It remains the benchmark in modern finance. My intuition pointed somewhere else, though.

People subconsciously know they have finite wealth.

The astronomical prizes behind the infinite expectation only arrive after long strings of losses (and only if the casino has unbounded credit, which is unrealistic in itself). Most people know their stake would be gone long before that lucky streak showed up.

A Simulation of Finite Stakes

To test this, I wrote a simulation with one crucial rule. Winnings cannot fund more plays. You arrive with a fixed stake, and when it is gone, your game is over. Call this the stake-based model. How does a player’s chance of breaking even change across starting stakes and entry prices?

Click to see the simulation code 
import random

def simulate_stake_play(start_stake, entry_price):
    stake = float(start_stake)
    net_winnings = 0.0
    
    while stake >= entry_price:
        stake -= entry_price
        
        # Flip until heads
        flips = 1
        while random.random() > 0.5:
            flips += 1
        
        payout = 2**flips
        net_winnings += payout
    
    return net_winnings + stake

def generate_results_table():
    entry_prices = [6, 8, 10, 13]
    wealth_levels = [64, 256, 1024, 8192]
    n_sims = 50_000

    header = "| Starting Stake | " + " | ".join([f"Price = ${p}" for p in entry_prices]) + " |"
    separator = "|:---" + "|:---" * len(entry_prices) + "|"
    print("## Chance of Breaking Even or Profiting\n")
    print(header)
    print(separator)

    for wealth in wealth_levels:
        row = [f"**${wealth:,}**"]
        
        for price in entry_prices:
            if wealth < price:
                row.append("N/A")
                continue

            outcomes = [simulate_stake_play(wealth, price) for _ in range(n_sims)]
            success_rate = sum(1 for outcome in outcomes if outcome >= wealth) / n_sims
            row.append(f"{success_rate * 100:.1f}%")

        print("| " + " | ".join(row) + " |")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    generate_results_table()

Chance of Breaking Even or Profiting

Starting Stake Price = $6 Price = $8 Price = $10 Price = $13
$64 49.9% 31.2% 21.6% 14.5%
$256 73.7% 45.9% 31.0% 19.1%
$1,024 95.6% 67.4% 44.0% 26.1%
$8,192 100.0% 98.0% 75.6% 41.1%

An exact calculation, which convolves the payout distribution instead of sampling it, agrees with every cell to within half a percentage point. Read across a row and the odds collapse as the price rises. Read down a column and a bigger stake buys far better odds at the same price. The game is not the same for everyone.

Ergodicity Economics

This line of thinking led me to the physicist Ole Peters and the field of ergodicity economics, which gave my intuition a name. On this view the problem is not psychology. It is the kind of average being used.

The ensemble average is the standard expected value \(\mathbb{E}[X]\), the average payout per player as more and more people play in parallel. Here it never settles. It creeps upward without bound, yet so slowly that a crowd of a million players would typically average only about $23 each. The infinity lives in outcomes too rare for any real crowd to see.

The time average follows one person’s wealth as they play again and again. That is the average we actually live through.

When the two coincide, the system is called ergodic. Here they don’t. Ergodicity economics argues that a rational person should maximize the long-term growth rate of their wealth, which for multiplicative processes means maximizing the expected change in log-wealth.

Notice what this does and doesn’t change. The resulting condition is mathematically identical to Bernoulli’s logarithmic utility, as Peters himself says in his abstract. What differs is the justification. The logarithm now comes from the dynamics of repeated play rather than from an assumption about how people feel about money.

That difference can be tested. If the logarithm comes from the dynamics, risk attitudes should shift when the dynamics shift. A 2021 lab study by Meder and colleagues found risk aversion rising under multiplicative dynamics, roughly as the time-optimal model predicts. One study proves little on its own. Still, it is a genuine test.

There is a caveat, too. The framework matches the growth measure to the dynamics, using the logarithm when wealth compounds and the plain average when gains simply add up. In the stake-based game, gains add up. Applied literally there, the framework hands back the plain average, which never settles, so in that game the finite stake is what keeps the price finite. Peters’ logarithm needs the extra assumption that the gamble sits inside a wealth process that compounds. For most people that is reasonable, but it remains an assumption.

The Exact Growth-Neutral Price

A price c is “growth-neutral” if it leaves expected log-wealth unchanged. For a player with total wealth W who reinvests their winnings (with c ≤ W), the condition reads

\[\mathbb{E}[\Delta \log(W)] = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} p_n \cdot \log(W - c + \text{payout}_n) - \log(W) = 0\]

With \(p_n = 1/2^n\) and a payout of \(2^n\) (taking $1 as the unit for the first head), this becomes

\[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^n} \log(W - c + 2^n) = \log(W)\]

There is no closed form for c. Solving it numerically is easy, though, and for large wealth a simple approximation emerges.

Approximate Rule

Think about the toss k at which the payout first matches your wealth, so 2^k ≈ W and k ≈ log₂(W). Outcomes well below this crossover barely move your wealth. Each adds about \(\frac{1}{2^n} \cdot \frac{2^n}{W} = \frac{1}{W}\) to the expected log-growth, which is the same dollar per outcome that makes the classical expectation diverge, now scaled by your wealth. There are about \(\log_2 W\) of them. Outcomes past the crossover multiply your wealth, but they are rare enough to add only a bounded amount, and the entry price costs about \(c/W\). Balance the books and you get

\[c^*(W) \approx \log_2(W) + \frac{1}{\ln 2} - \frac{1}{2} \approx \log_2(W) + 0.943\]

In other words, the fair price is roughly the expected payout over the outcomes that pay less than your wealth, one dollar each, plus a constant for the rest.

The constant comes out exactly. For \(c \ll W\) the price enters as \(-c/W\), so \(c^*\) is close to

\[S(W) = W \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^n} \ln\left(1 + \frac{2^n}{W}\right) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} g(n - \log_2 W), \qquad g(x) = 2^{-x}\ln(1 + 2^x).\]

Since \(g\) tends to 1 for small outcomes and to 0 for large ones, the Euler-Maclaurin formula gives one unit per small outcome, a boundary correction of \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\), and the integral \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \big(g(x) - \mathbf{1}[x \le 0]\big)\,dx = \tfrac{1}{\ln 2}\). (Substitute \(u = 2^x\) and the remaining integral is exactly 1.) The leftover error is periodic in \(\log_2 W\) and of order \(10^{-12}\).

The approximation drops terms of order \(c^2/W\). At $64 it gives $6.94 against an exact $7.21, and by $8,192 the two agree within a cent. My earlier rule of thumb, log₂(W) + 1, stays within about 20 cents over this range, but the offset is not really 1. It falls from 1.21 at $64 toward 0.943.

Either way, the price is finite and depends directly on wealth.

Three Prices, Two Yardsticks

So what is the fair price for the stake-based game we simulated? An earlier version of this post fell into a trap here. “Fair” needs a definition, and the formula and the simulation suggest different ones. The growth-neutral equation uses a log-growth yardstick, under which expected log-wealth stays put. The simulation suggests a median yardstick, the price that gives you even odds of leaving with at least what you came with.

The median price turns out to be easy to compute exactly. A stake W at price c buys N = ⌊W/c⌋ games and leaves W − Nc in change. You walk away with at least W precisely when your total payout reaches Nc, which means your average payout per game has to cover the ticket price. The change drops out entirely. Instead of searching by simulation, we can convolve the payout distribution N times and read off the answer.

Click to see the price code 
import math
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq


def growth_neutral_price(W):
    """Price c with E[log(W - c + payout)] = log(W) for one play (payout 2^n w.p. 2^-n)."""
    n = np.arange(1, 200)
    excess_log_growth = lambda c: np.sum(0.5**n * np.log1p((2.0**n - c) / W))
    return brentq(excess_log_growth, 0.0, W)


def median_fair_price(W):
    """Exact largest price c at which a stake-based player with stake W
    has at least a 50% chance of walking away with >= W.

    With N = floor(W / c) games, walking away with >= W  <=>  total payout S_N >= N * c,
    so we only need the distribution of S_N (capped at W, which loses nothing here)."""
    payouts = []                          # (payout, probability); payouts >= W lumped at W
    n = 1
    while 2**n < W:
        payouts.append((2**n, 0.5**n))
        n += 1
    payouts.append((W, 0.5**(n - 1)))

    dist = np.zeros(W + 1)
    dist[0] = 1.0                         # distribution of min(S_N, W), starting at N = 0
    best_price, best_games, games = 0.0, 0, 0
    while True:
        games += 1
        if W / games <= best_price:       # c <= W / N, so no larger price is possible
            return best_price, best_games
        new = np.zeros(W + 1)
        for v, p in payouts:              # add one more game
            new[v:] += p * dist[:W + 1 - v]
            new[W] += p * dist[W + 1 - v:].sum()
        dist = new
        tail = np.cumsum(dist[::-1])[::-1]          # tail[k] = P(S_N >= k)
        m = np.nonzero(tail >= 0.5)[0].max()        # largest m with P(S_N >= m) >= 1/2
        price = m / games
        if price > W / (games + 1) and price > best_price:   # consistent with N = floor(W/c)
            best_price, best_games = price, games


def log_fair_stake_price(W, n_paths=200_000, step=0.005, seed=0):
    """Largest price c (on a grid) with E[log(final wealth)] >= log(W) in the stake-based
    game, where final wealth = S_N + leftover and N = floor(W / c). Monte Carlo."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    games_needed = {}
    for c in np.arange(math.log2(W) - 2.5, math.log2(W) + 2.0, step):
        games = int(W // c)
        games_needed.setdefault(games, []).append((c, W - games * c))
    total = np.zeros(n_paths)
    best = 0.0
    for games in range(1, max(games_needed) + 1):
        total += 2.0 ** rng.geometric(0.5, n_paths)   # play one more game on every path
        for c, leftover in games_needed.get(games, []):
            if np.mean(np.log(total + leftover)) >= math.log(W):
                best = max(best, c)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("| Starting Stake | Growth-neutral, compounding (exact) "
          "| Log yardstick, stake-based (simulated) | Median yardstick, stake-based (exact) |")
    print("|:---|:---|:---|:---|")
    for W in [64, 256, 1024, 8192]:
        median_price, _ = median_fair_price(W)
        print(f"| **${W:,}** | ${growth_neutral_price(W):.2f} "
              f"| ${log_fair_stake_price(W):.2f} | ${median_price:.2f} |")

    print()
    print("| Starting Stake | Games N | Median price | Median price − log₂N | Gap to growth-neutral |")
    print("|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|")
    for W in [64, 256, 1024, 8192, 65536]:
        price, games = median_fair_price(W)
        print(f"| **${W:,}** | {games:,} | ${price:.2f} | {price - math.log2(games):.2f} "
              f"| ${growth_neutral_price(W) - price:.2f} |")
Starting Stake Growth-neutral, compounding (exact) Log yardstick, stake-based (simulated) Median yardstick, stake-based (exact)
$64 $7.21 $7.02 $5.82
$256 $9.06 $8.85 $7.64
$1,024 $10.99 $10.78 $9.34
$8,192 $13.95 $13.81 $11.99

The simulated column uses 200,000 paths and is accurate to about 3 cents. The other two are exact.

Under the same log-growth yardstick, the stake-based rules cost only 14 to 21 cents relative to compounding. Switching yardsticks costs more than a dollar at every stake. Why so much? The median only asks whether you broke even and ignores how far a jackpot carries you past that point. The log yardstick credits jackpots, damped by the logarithm, and with payouts this lopsided that difference is large.

Why the Gap Widens with Wealth

The median price follows a law of its own. Feller (1945, Annals of Mathematical Statistics) proved that the total payout from N St. Petersburg games satisfies \(S_N/(N \log_2 N) \to 1\) in probability, and Martin-Löf (1985) later described the limiting distribution of these sums. The typical average payout per game grows like log₂N. A stake-based player gets N = W/c games, so the median price should be log₂N plus a constant.

Starting Stake Games N Median price Median price − log₂N Gap to growth-neutral
$64 11 $5.82 2.36 $1.39
$256 33 $7.64 2.59 $1.42
$1,024 109 $9.34 2.57 $1.65
$8,192 683 $11.99 2.57 $1.96
$65,536 4,454 $14.71 2.59 $2.23

Past the smallest stake, the constant sits near 2.6. At a stake of about $1 million, with roughly 57,000 games, it is still 2.60. Substituting N = W/c gives

\[c_{\text{median}} \approx \log_2 W - \log_2 \log_2 W + 2.6\]

which grows more slowly than the growth-neutral price \(\log_2 W + 0.943\). So the gap widens with wealth instead of shrinking, roughly like \(\log_2 \log_2 W\), and reaches $2.54 at about $1 million.

The same law explains the million-player crowd from earlier. With N = 1,000,000, log₂N is about 20, and adding 2.6 gives roughly $22.5, close to the $23 median I got from simulating 400 such crowds.

Conclusion

The paradox dissolves once you pin down two things, how the game is played and what “fair” means. Model a player with finite wealth playing through time, and the price turns finite and personal, about log₂(W) + 0.94 dollars by the growth-neutral yardstick.

Does that make utility theory unnecessary? That is a question of interpretation, not arithmetic. The growth-neutral condition is Bernoulli’s equation, and ergodicity economics changes the reason for the logarithm rather than the price it produces. Economists have pushed back on the stronger claims (Doctor, Wakker & Wang, 2020), although Peters’ reading makes a testable prediction that Bernoulli’s does not.

The simulation adds one more lesson. A player who just wants even odds should pay less still, and that discount grows with wealth. The value of the game depends on your circumstances, the rules you play under, and the yardstick you choose.

Revision note (October 2026). An earlier version labeled log₂(W) + 1 as exact and treated the gap between a log-growth price and a median price as a cost of the game rules. It also had a “total ruin” variant whose apparent premium came from leftover change, so I removed it.

entry.title: The Button Game: When Should You Stop for the Best Prize?

link.title: The Button Game: When Should You Stop for the Best Prize?

entry.content:
An Interview Puzzle

While preparing for an upcoming technical interview, I came across a probability puzzle that, at first glance, seems like a simple game of chance, but quickly reveals layers of strategic depth. The problem was as follows:

An agent can press a button up to 10 times. Each press generates a random monetary value, drawn from a continuous uniform distribution on the interval [0, $100,000]. After each press, the agent can either stop and keep the current value, ending the game, or discard the value and continue to the next press. If the agent completes all 10 presses, they must accept the value from the 10th press.

The question is: What is the optimal strategy to maximize the expected payoff?

My initial intuition was to work backward from the end. But after solving it, I became more interested in the bigger picture: what kind of problem is this, and what mathematical principles guarantee that the solution is truly optimal?

Zooming Out: The World of Optimal Stopping

This puzzle is not a one-off brain teaser; it’s a classic example of a finite-horizon optimal stopping problem. This class of problems is fundamental in fields like finance, economics, and computer science, dealing with the challenge of choosing the perfect time to take a particular action to maximize a reward or minimize a cost.

To analyze such problems rigorously, we model them as Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). An MDP is a mathematical framework for decision-making in situations where outcomes are partly random and partly under the control of a decision-maker. Our game fits this framework perfectly:

  1. States: The state at any point is the number of presses remaining, \(n\), together with the value \(x\) we just drew.
  2. Actions: In any state (where \(n > 1\)), our actions are to stop or continue.
  3. The Markov Property: Most importantly, the game is “memoryless.” Because each press is independent of the others, the history of previously rejected values carries no information about future draws. The decision with \(n\) presses left depends only on \(n\) and the value \(x\) in hand.

Recognizing the problem as an MDP is the first step, as it allows us to bring a powerful toolkit to bear on finding the solution: the theory of dynamic programming.

Dynamic Programming and Bellman’s Principle

The cornerstone for solving MDPs is dynamic programming, a method for breaking down a complex problem into a sequence of simpler, nested subproblems. The philosophical foundation of this method is Bellman’s Principle of Optimality.

Bellman’s Principle of Optimality states that an optimal policy has the property that whatever the initial state and first decision are, the remaining decisions must constitute an optimal policy for the subproblem starting from the new state.

In simpler terms, a perfect overall plan is composed of a series of perfect sub-plans. To play the 10-press game optimally, our strategy for the remaining 9 presses (should we continue) must also be the optimal strategy for a 9-press game.

This principle is captured mathematically in the Bellman Equation. For our type of optimal stopping problem, the equation takes the following form. If we let \(V_n\) be the maximum expected payoff we can get with \(n\) presses remaining, then:

\[V_n = \mathbb{E}[\max(X_n, V_{n-1})]\]

This elegant equation is the blueprint for our strategy. It says the value of being in a state with \(n\) presses left is the expected value of the best possible choice: either the random value \(X_n\) we just drew, or the value \(V_{n-1}\) we expect to get if we discard the current draw and play optimally from the next state.

Applying the Theory to Solve the Puzzle

With this theoretical framework, we can now solve the interview puzzle methodically using backward induction. For clarity, let’s set \(C = 100,000\).

Step 1: Solve the Base Case (\(n=1\)) We start at the end. With only one press left, we must accept the outcome. The expected value is the mean of the uniform distribution: \(V_1 = \mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{C}{2} = \$50,000\)

Step 2: Derive the General Recurrence Relation For any stage \(n \ge 2\), the decision rule is to stop if the draw \(x\) is greater than the continuation value, \(V_{n-1}\). We can find the value \(V_n\) by calculating the expectation from the Bellman Equation:

\[V_n = \mathbb{E}[\max(X, V_{n-1})] = \int_{0}^{C} \max(x, V_{n-1}) \frac{dx}{C}\]

We split the integral at the threshold \(V_{n-1}\), since the value of \(\max(x, V_{n-1})\) changes at that point:

\[V_n = \frac{1}{C} \left[ \int_{0}^{V_{n-1}} V_{n-1} \,dx + \int_{V_{n-1}}^{C} x \,dx \right]\]

Now, we solve the integrals:

\[V_n = \frac{1}{C} \left[ V_{n-1} [x]_0^{V_{n-1}} + \left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_{V_{n-1}}^C \right]\] \[V_n = \frac{1}{C} \left[ V_{n-1}(V_{n-1} - 0) + \left(\frac{C^2}{2} - \frac{V_{n-1}^2}{2}\right) \right]\] \[V_n = \frac{1}{C} \left[ V_{n-1}^2 + \frac{C^2 - V_{n-1}^2}{2} \right] = \frac{2V_{n-1}^2 + C^2 - V_{n-1}^2}{2C}\]

This simplifies to the clean, general recurrence relation we can use for all steps:

\[V_n = \frac{V_{n-1}^2 + C^2}{2C}\]

Using this formula, we can now iterate backward from our known base case (\(V_1 = 50,000\)) to generate the complete optimal strategy. For instance:

  • For n=2: \(V_2 = \frac{(50000)^2 + (100000)^2}{2 \cdot 100000} = \$62,500\)
  • For n=3: \(V_3 = \frac{(62500)^2 + (100000)^2}{2 \cdot 100000} \approx \$69,531\)

Repeating this process for all 10 stages gives us the following policy:

Presses Left (n) Threshold to Stop (\(V_{n-1}\)) Expected Payoff (\(V_n\))
10 $84,982 $86,110
9 $83,645 $84,982
8 $82,030 $83,645
7 $80,038 $82,030
6 $77,508 $80,038
5 $74,173 $77,508
4 $69,531 $74,173
3 $62,500 $69,531
2 $50,000 $62,500
1 (Must accept draw) $50,000

Note: Dollar values are rounded to the nearest dollar.

Empirical Validation with Python Simulation

As a final check, a Monte Carlo simulation confirms that this strategy works in practice.

Implementation

import random

def calculate_thresholds(max_presses, C=100000):
    V = {}
    V[1] = C / 2
    for n in range(2, max_presses + 1):
        V_n_minus_1 = V[n - 1]
        V[n] = (V_n_minus_1**2 + C**2) / (2 * C)
    return V

def play_one_game(thresholds, max_presses, C=100000):
    for presses_left in range(max_presses, 0, -1):
        current_draw = random.uniform(0, C)
        if presses_left == 1:
            return current_draw
        threshold = thresholds[presses_left - 1]
        if current_draw >= threshold:
            return current_draw
    return 0 

def main():
    MAX_PRESSES = 10
    C = 100000
    NUM_SIMULATIONS = 1_000_000
    thresholds = calculate_thresholds(MAX_PRESSES, C)
    print(f"Theoretical Expected Payoff: ${thresholds[MAX_PRESSES]:,.2f}\n")
    total_payoff = sum(play_one_game(thresholds, MAX_PRESSES, C) for _ in range(NUM_SIMULATIONS))
    average_payoff = total_payoff / NUM_SIMULATIONS
    print(f"Simulated Average Payoff ({NUM_SIMULATIONS:,} games): ${average_payoff:,.2f}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Results

Theoretical Expected Payoff: $86,109.82

Simulated Average Payoff (1,000,000 games): $86,112.80

The simulated average differs from the theoretical value by less than 3 dollars. With a million games, the Monte Carlo standard error is about 14 dollars, so the agreement is as close as we should expect.

Why the Strategy is Optimal

This brings us to the decisive question: why is this threshold rule not merely good, but provably optimal? Because the game has a finite horizon, backward induction is itself the proof.

The argument runs by induction on the number of presses left:

  • Base case. With one press left there is no decision to make, so \(V_1 = C/2\) is the best achievable expected payoff.
  • Inductive step. Suppose \(V_{n-1}\) is the best expected payoff any strategy can achieve with \(n-1\) presses left. With \(n\) presses left and a draw \(x\) in hand, a strategy can either stop and receive \(x\), or continue.
    • Future draws are independent of everything seen so far, so continuing starts a fresh \((n-1)\)-press game. By assumption, no strategy can expect more than \(V_{n-1}\) in that game.
    • So from this point no strategy can expect more than \(\max(x, V_{n-1})\), and the threshold rule achieves exactly that.
    • Averaging over \(x\) shows that \(V_n = \mathbb{E}[\max(X, V_{n-1})]\) is the best achievable value with \(n\) presses left.

By induction, the rule “stop when the draw \(x \ge V_{n-1}\)” is optimal at every stage. No strategy, however elaborate, can beat the expected payoff \(V_{10} \approx 86{,}110\). This is Bellman’s Principle of Optimality at work. The best plan for the 10-press game is built from the best plans for every shorter game.

The same conclusion is a small instance of a general result from optimal stopping theory. The values \(\max(x, V_{n-1})\) form the Snell envelope of the payoff process, which is the smallest supermartingale that dominates it. A classical theorem says that stopping the first time the payoff equals its Snell envelope is optimal. Here, that is exactly the first draw with \(x \ge V_{n-1}\).

Updated October 2026: this section previously appealed to the Bellman operator being a contraction with a unique fixed point. That argument is the tool for infinite-horizon, discounted problems, where there is no last step to start from. For a finite horizon like this one, backward induction from the last press is the proof.

entry.title: Exploring PCA and Sparse PCA on Intraday S&P 500 Returns

link.title: Exploring PCA and Sparse PCA on Intraday S&P 500 Returns

entry.content:
A Note from 2026

I wrote this post in October 2024, shortly after finishing my M.S., as a hands-on way to learn PCA and Sparse PCA on real market data. Re-reading it two years later, the data pipeline and the plots hold up, but much of the original interpretation does not. I read macro and geopolitical stories into six weeks of 2-minute returns, and some of the methods had problems I did not catch at the time.

In October 2026 I revised the text. The code and data are unchanged, and so is every figure except the rolling-window dashboard, where I fixed a labeling bug (see below). The edits are to the writing, plus a few quick checks against the outputs saved in the project repository; nothing was re-run. The original title was “Detecting Regime Shifts in SP500 Stocks Using PCA and Sparse PCA”. I changed it because the project explores structure; it does not detect regime shifts.

What changed in this revision:

  • I removed the macro and geopolitical narratives (sanctions, BRICS, defense spending, “market complacency”). Nothing in this analysis can test them.
  • I corrected readings that depended on the arbitrary sign of principal components. These include the negative correlations with the volatility ETN (VXX), which reflect the ordinary negative relationship between stock returns and volatility. They say nothing about how much risk the market was pricing.
  • I corrected factual details:
    • the sample length and dates;
    • the number of components needed for 90% of the variance;
    • the description of the ETF set;
    • which windows had the lowest similarity to the full period;
    • the size of the largest lagged correlations;
    • a few percentages in the sector tables and intraday plots.
  • I fixed a labeling bug in the rolling-window dashboard. Once the slider moved, the sector names no longer matched the rows. My original reading of that figure was based on the wrong labels, so I re-read the observations in that section from the underlying data.
  • I added caveats where the method limits what can be concluded. I also removed the “Implications” sections on trading, liquidity provision and rebalancing, which the analysis does not support.

What I would do differently today:

  1. Remove the overnight gap. The first 2-minute return of each day spans the overnight move from the previous close. Those 28 returns account for roughly a quarter of the total variance in the standardized data. They change the full-period results only modestly, but they dominate the 9:30-10:00 bucket in the intraday analysis.
  2. Compare against a noise baseline. With 457 stocks and about 5,500 observations, random matrix theory (the Marchenko-Pastur distribution) gives the range of eigenvalues that pure noise would produce. A back-of-the-envelope check suggests only about 30 components clear the upper edge of that range. Most of the 255 components needed for 90% of the variance are therefore indistinguishable from noise.
  3. Tune the sparsity penalty. I used sklearn’s default, and the resulting “sparse” components still load on most stocks.
  4. Align components before comparing them across fits. The sign and order of components are arbitrary in every fit. Windows should be matched first, by sign or by comparing subspaces through principal angles, before measuring any change in structure.
  5. Test before calling something a regime shift. A bootstrap or permutation null for the stability metric is needed to say whether a dip is unusual. Without one, the rolling-window results are descriptive.
  6. Use enough data per fit. Each intraday bucket has fewer observations (420) than stocks (457), so its sample covariance matrix is singular.

Introduction

This project applies Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Sparse PCA to high-frequency returns of S&P 500 stocks. The goal was exploratory. I wanted to see:

  • what structure these techniques pick up in 2-minute data;
  • how that structure lines up with sectors and sector ETFs;
  • whether it visibly changes over a few weeks that included the Federal Reserve’s first rate cut of the cycle (September 18, 2024).

PCA is a standard tool for this kind of data. It compresses hundreds of correlated return series into a handful of components, the first of which usually tracks the market as a whole. Sparse PCA adds a penalty that pushes many loadings to zero, which can make components easier to read.

The raw download covers all 503 S&P 500 constituents and 20 ETFs at 2-minute intervals from the Yahoo Finance API. After cleaning, the sample is 457 stocks over 28 full trading days, from August 12 to September 19, 2024.

The project was also a way for me to practice end-to-end machine learning work on real data: acquisition, cleaning, modeling and interactive visualization. It is best read as an exploration, not as a set of trading conclusions.

Data Preparation

Data Verification and Consistency

The download included all 503 S&P 500 stocks and 20 ETFs at 2-minute intervals. Yahoo Finance only provides 2-minute bars for roughly the last 60 days, which limited the sample length.

I kept regular market hours only, from 9:30 AM to 4:00 PM ET. This gives 195 bars per trading day and avoids the thin, irregular trading of the pre-market and after-hours sessions.

Data Cleaning and Preprocessing

The data cleaning process involved the following steps:

  1. Handling Missing Data: I filled short gaps forward and then backward, up to 5 intervals, and dropped any rows that were still incomplete. In hindsight this has two side effects. Backward filling uses later prices to fill earlier gaps, and every filled price creates an artificial zero return. With a 5-interval limit the effect is probably small, but today I would mask these points instead.

  2. Asset Filtering: I removed any asset with more than 20% missing data. This kept 457 of the 503 stocks.

  3. Timestamp Synchronization: All series were aligned to a common time index, so that price movements are compared at the same moments across the dataset.

  4. Return Calculation: I worked with logarithmic returns rather than prices. Log returns are additive over time and closely approximate percentage changes over short intervals. Because the returns were computed on the stitched-together series, the first return of each day spans the overnight gap (see the note at the top).

  5. Standardization: I standardized each stock’s return series to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. This keeps stocks with different volatilities on a comparable scale.

The cleaned dataset has 5,463 synchronized timestamps, about 97% of the 5,655 in the raw download. These give 5,462 2-minute returns for 457 stocks and 20 ETFs. A handful of stocks have no data on the first day of the download (August 9), so dropping incomplete rows removes almost all of that day. The analyzed sample therefore effectively runs from August 12 to September 19.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA transforms a dataset into a new coordinate system whose axes, the principal components, are ordered by how much variance they explain. This section covers three steps:

  • standard PCA on the full sample;
  • Sparse PCA;
  • a sector-level summary of the Sparse PCA loadings.

Full Period PCA

I applied PCA to the full sample of 457 stocks. PCA finds a set of orthogonal directions (the principal components) that maximize the variance of the projected data.

For a data matrix $X$, PCA solves the eigenvalue problem:

\[(X^TX)v_i = \lambda_i v_i\]

where $v_i$ are the eigenvectors (principal components) and $\lambda_i$ are the corresponding eigenvalues, which measure the variance explained by each component.

Components are ordered by decreasing explained variance, so PC1 explains the most, PC2 the second most, and so on.

I used sklearn’s PCA implementation and kept enough components to explain 90% of the variance.

Interpretation of Full Period PCA Results

The cumulative explained variance plot shows how quickly variance is captured. The first component alone explains about 24.5% of the variance and the second about 7.4%. After that the curve flattens: 154 components are needed for 80% of the variance, and 255 (slightly more than half of the 457) for 90%.

That long tail is expected at this frequency. Over 2-minute intervals, much of each stock’s return is idiosyncratic noise and market microstructure (bid-ask bounce, asynchronous trading). Correlations between stocks are also weaker than at daily frequency, a pattern known as the Epps effect. So one large market component followed by a long, flat tail is the typical picture, and many of the trailing components are likely indistinguishable from noise (see the note at the top).

PC1 has a positive loading on every stock and behaves like a market factor. Beyond the first few components, principal components usually mix several influences. They should not be read as clean economic factors without further work.

Sparse PCA

Standard PCA components involve every input variable, which makes them hard to interpret. Sparse PCA adds a penalty that pushes many loadings to exactly zero, so that each component is described by fewer stocks.

In sklearn’s formulation, Sparse PCA solves:

\[\min_{U,V} \frac{1}{2}\lVert X - UV \rVert_F^2 + \alpha \lVert V \rVert_{1} \quad \text{subject to } \lVert U_k \rVert_2 \le 1 \text{ for all } k\]

Here the rows of $V$ are the components, that is, the loadings over stocks, which are the part being made sparse. $U$ holds the corresponding component scores over time, and $\alpha$ controls the strength of the sparsity penalty.

I used sklearn’s SparsePCA with 10 components and the default penalty, $\alpha = 1$. Two things about the result matter for everything that follows:

  • The components are only mildly sparse. With the default penalty, each component still has non-zero loadings on roughly 340 to 400 of the 457 stocks. The components end up tilted toward particular sectors rather than isolating a small group of stocks. I should have tuned $\alpha$.
  • The components are not ordered by explained variance. Unlike standard PCA, sklearn’s SparsePCA does not sort them, so the labels PC1 to PC10 are just labels. For example, Sparse PC9 is not the ninth most important component.

In principle, Sparse PCA trades some explained variance for interpretability. The main practical drawbacks are:

  • the result depends on the choice of $\alpha$;
  • it is more expensive to fit than standard PCA;
  • its components are not orthogonal or ranked the way standard principal components are.

Correlation with ETF Factors

To connect the components to something observable, I correlated each component’s scores with the returns of 20 ETFs:

  • broad-market funds: SPY, QQQ, DIA and IWM;
  • the SPDR sector funds: XLK, XLV, XLF, XLE, XLI, XLP, XLY, XLU, XLB, XLRE and XLC;
  • a short-term VIX futures ETN: VXX;
  • gold, silver, oil and long-term Treasury funds: GLD, SLV, USO and TLT.

Methodology

  1. Component Scores: I projected the standardized stock returns onto the PCA and Sparse PCA loadings to get a time series of scores for each component.

  2. Correlation Analysis: I computed Pearson correlations between each component’s scores and each ETF’s standardized returns.

  3. Visualization: The correlations are shown as heatmaps.

  4. Lag Analysis: To look for leading or lagging relationships, I repeated the correlations with the ETF returns shifted by up to 5 intervals (10 minutes) in either direction.

Rolling Window PCA

To look at how the structure evolves, I repeated the analysis on rolling windows.

Methodology

I applied both standard PCA and Sparse PCA using rolling windows with the following parameters:

  1. Window Size: 10 trading days (1,950 2-minute returns)
  2. Step Size: 1 trading day (195 returns)
  3. Number of Components: 10

This gives 19 windows. Each is labeled by its last day, from August 23 to September 19. Consecutive windows share nine of their ten days, so they are expected to look similar.

For each window, I:

  1. extracted the data for the window;
  2. fitted standard PCA and Sparse PCA;
  3. computed sector loadings for each of the first 10 components;
  4. compared the result with the previous window and with the full sample.

Stability and Similarity Metrics

Both metrics are computed from the standard PCA results. For each of the first 10 components, I took the sector shares of its positive loadings (the same construction as in the intraday section below) and flattened them into a single vector.

  1. Market Stability compares consecutive windows using cosine similarity:

    \[\mathrm{Stability}_{i, i+1} = 1 - \mathrm{cosine\_distance}(\mathrm{loadings}_i, \mathrm{loadings}_{i+1})\]

    where $\mathrm{loadings}$ are the flattened sector-share vectors. Higher values mean consecutive windows look more alike.

  2. Similarity to the Full Period compares each window with the full-sample result:

    \[\mathrm{SimFull}_i = 1 - \mathrm{cosine\_distance}(\mathrm{loadings}_i, \mathrm{loadings}_{\mathrm{full}})\]

    In the dashboard this panel is labeled “Deviation from Full Period”. Despite that name, it is a similarity score: lower values mean the window looks less like the full sample.

Results and Interpretation

Sector Loadings Over Time

Stepping through the windows shows a few patterns. In the original version of the dashboard, the sector labels stopped matching the rows once the slider moved, and my original observations were read off those wrong labels. The figure is now fixed, and the observations below were re-read from the underlying data:

  1. Consumer early on: In every window ending August 23 to September 4, consumer stocks lead half or more of the ten standard-PCA components. Afterwards they lead three or fewer. Consumer is also the largest of my merged sectors, so it tends to lead whenever loadings are spread evenly. This is partly a sector-size effect.

  2. Technology and utilities in PC2: Utilities lead standard PC2 in the first five windows (ending August 23 to 29) and again in the last one. Technology leads it in every window from August 30 to September 18 except September 3, at 44-54%. In Sparse PCA, PC2 mostly alternates between the same two sectors.

  3. Energy in PC3: Energy leads PC3 in both methods from late August to mid-September, at 32-49%. In standard PCA that is the windows ending August 30 to September 12; in Sparse PCA, August 29 to September 16.

  4. Financial Services in PC1: Financial services leads Sparse PC1 in every window ending August 30 to September 16. It also leads standard PC1 in the windows ending September 11 to 17, but only with 17-18%. Standard PC1 is the market factor, so its loadings are spread across all sectors.

  5. Real Estate and Healthcare later: Real estate leads PC4 in both methods in the windows ending September 13 to 19. From early September, healthcare leads one or more of the later components in most windows.

These observations are descriptive. The sign and order of components can change from one window to the next. Some of these shifts may therefore reflect a component flipping sign or swapping places with another, rather than a real change in market structure.

Market Stability

The stability values range from 0.76 to 0.97, and most are above 0.8.

  • Lowest values: the windows ending August 30 (0.771), September 12 (0.771) and September 19 (0.763).
  • Highest values: September 6 and September 16 (both 0.972).

In the original version I matched each dip to a news event, such as a producer-price inflation release on September 12 and the Fed’s decision on September 18. I no longer think the metric supports that, for two reasons:

  1. Sign flips. The metric counts only positive loadings. If a component flips sign between windows, the metric counts the other half of its stocks, and this registers as a change in structure. Every component except PC1 flips sign at least twice over the 18 steps.
  2. A high floor. Converting loadings into sector shares pulls everything toward the same baseline. Even completely unstructured loadings would produce shares that roughly mirror sector sizes, and two windows of random loadings would look nearly identical. A high value therefore does not mean stable structure. It can also mean there is no sector concentration at all.

A quick check against the saved loadings makes both points concrete:

  • Aligning each component’s sign with the previous window removes the September 12 dip entirely: 0.77 becomes 0.92.
  • Replacing the loadings with random numbers gives values around 0.97, the same level as the “peak stability” readings.

After sign alignment, the lowest values are at the steps into the windows ending September 18 and 19, which add the day of the Fed’s 50 basis point cut (WSJ, Sept. 18, 2024) and the day after. August 30 is nearly as low, though. Without a null distribution, I would not call any of this a regime shift.

Similarity to the Full Period

Similarity to the full sample generally declines over the period. It ranges from about 0.69 to 0.85 in the windows ending before September 13, and from 0.54 to 0.59 in the windows ending September 13 to 19. The window most similar to the full sample is the one ending September 3 (0.849).

One possible explanation is that the last week of the sample, which contains the Fed decision, differs from the rest. However, the same caveats about sign flips and the missing baseline apply, so I treat this as a descriptive observation rather than a finding.

Takeaways

The rolling-window analysis is a useful way to visualize how loadings move around over a short sample. In its current form it is not a regime-shift detector. Making it one would need component alignment across windows and a null distribution for the metrics. The result also depends on the window length, and with heavily overlapping windows, consecutive values are not independent.

Intraday Pattern Analysis

Next I looked at whether sector structure differs by time of day. Intraday patterns such as heavier trading at the open and close are well documented, so it seemed worth checking whether they show up in the components.

Methodology

  1. Data Segmentation: I divided the trading day into 13 periods of 30 minutes each:

    \[p_i = [t_i, t_{i+1}), \quad i = 1, 2, ..., 13\]

    where $t_1$ is the market open (9:30 AM) and $t_{14}$ the market close (4:00 PM).

  2. Sparse PCA Application: For each period $p_i$, I pooled the returns from that half hour across all days and fitted Sparse PCA with 10 components:

    \[X_{p_i} \approx U_{p_i} V_{p_i}\]

    where $X_{p_i}$ is the data matrix for period $p_i$, the rows of $V_{p_i}$ are the sparse loadings, and $U_{p_i}$ holds the component scores.

  3. Sector Loading Calculation: For each component $j$ and sector $S$ in period $p_i$, the sector loading $SL_{S,j,p_i}$ is:

    \[SL_{S,j,p_i} = \sum_{k \in S} \max(L_{k,j,p_i}, 0)\]

    where $L_{k,j,p_i}$ is the loading of stock $k$ in component $j$ for period $p_i$. These were then normalized across sectors:

    \[NSL_{S,j,p_i} = \frac{SL_{S,j,p_i}}{\sum_{S'} SL_{S',j,p_i}}\]

  4. Visualization: I produced two charts:

    • an intraday heatmap showing $NSL_{S,j,p_i}$ for all sectors, components and periods;

    • a sector influence plot showing each sector’s average influence:

      \[ASI_{S,p_i} = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{10} NSL_{S,j,p_i}}{\sum_{S'} \sum_{j=1}^{10} NSL_{S',j,p_i}}\]

Caveats (added in 2026). Four problems limit what this section can show:

  • Too few observations per fit. Each 30-minute bucket pools 15 returns per day over 28 days, so each Sparse PCA fit sees 420 observations of 457 stocks. With fewer observations than variables, the sample covariance matrix is singular and the fitted components are very noisy.
  • The overnight gap. The 9:30-10:00 bucket contains the 28 overnight-gap returns. These carry far more variance than ordinary 2-minute returns and dominate that bucket.
  • Arbitrary signs. As in the rolling-window section, only positive loadings are counted, so the results depend on arbitrary component signs.
  • Unrelated component numbers. Each bucket is a separate fit, so “PC3” at 10:00 and “PC3” at 14:00 need not be the same factor.

I would treat the figures below as a visualization of noisy fits rather than evidence of intraday patterns.

Limitations and Future Work

The main limitations of this section:

  1. Sample Size per Fit: Each period’s fit has fewer observations than stocks, which is the most serious limitation and is described above.

  2. Overnight Gap: The opening period mixes overnight moves with ordinary 2-minute returns.

  3. Time Period Specificity: The sample covers six weeks in August and September 2024 and may not generalize to other periods.

  4. Aggregation Effects: Pooling returns across days hides day-specific patterns, including responses to scheduled announcements.

  5. Sector Classification: The merged sector categories, especially the combined consumer category, are coarse.

A more convincing version of this analysis would:

  • use a much longer sample, so that each period’s fit has many more observations than stocks;
  • drop the overnight return, or treat the open separately;
  • compare each period with a baseline in which period labels are randomly shuffled, to see whether the differences exceed what noise produces;
  • check whether any pattern is stable across separate months.

Conclusion

What I think holds up:

  1. A single market factor dominates. PC1 explains about 24.5% of the variance, loads positively on every stock, and correlates at 0.85 or more with broad-market and cyclical-sector ETFs.
  2. Beyond PC1, the variance spectrum is long and flat. It takes 154 components for 80% of the variance and 255 for 90%. That is expected at 2-minute frequency, where much of the variation is noise.
  3. Several components line up with individual sectors (utilities, energy, real estate, financials, technology), confirmed by their correlations with the matching sector ETFs. With the default penalty, though, the “sparse” components remain mostly market baskets tilted toward a sector.

What does not hold up:

  • The rolling-window and intraday results are descriptive only. The stability metric is sensitive to component sign flips and has a high floor, and the intraday fits have fewer observations than stocks. Neither supports claims about regime shifts or tradable intraday patterns.

The most useful thing this project taught me was how easy it is to over-read PCA on market data. If I return to it, the list in the note at the top is where I would start.

Appendix
